alternatives: Use a framework renderer that escapes values by default.
userDecisions: Confirm which markup is a product requirement and where its trust boundary belongs.
rules.plainLanguage: Browser code inserts a value as HTML instead of text. If that value came from outside the app, it can change the page or run script.
rules.consequence: A successful path may steal in-page data, perform actions as the user or present false content.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule finds direct innerHTML/outerHTML assignments and append assignments, insertAdjacentHTML, and document.write/document.writeln calls. It does not trace input or determine sanitization.
rules.applicability: Non-test, non-generated browser JavaScript and TypeScript source files.
falsePositiveCauses: Only a fixed trusted literal reaches the sink.
The value is sanitized by a policy the lexical rule cannot identify.

proposal.summary: Use textContent or DOM construction for text, or sanitize required HTML with a reviewed allowlist at the trust boundary.

proposalRisks: Switching from HTML to text or allowlisted DOM nodes can alter formatting.
sideEffects: Legacy widgets or rich content may render differently.
rules.securityRetest: Pass a harmless HTML/script marker through the owned source and verify it is displayed as text or safely removed.
rules.functionalRetest: Exercise the affected page and compare intended text, formatting, links and interactive elements.
rules.rollback: Restore only the necessary formatting behavior if the UI regresses, while keeping untrusted markup out of executable HTML sinks.

alternatives: Define and test the health probe in the deployment platform instead of the reusable image.
userDecisions: Confirm whether the image is a long-running service and which endpoint or local command represents real readiness.
rules.plainLanguage: The image does not define a routine way for the container platform to tell whether the application is actually healthy.
rules.consequence: A stuck or partly started process may continue receiving traffic or remain unreplaced because the platform only knows that the process exists.
rules.confidenceBoundary: Checkov rule CKV_DOCKER_2 found no HEALTHCHECK in the Dockerfile. A deployment-level health probe may already exist and was not inspected.
rules.applicability: Files named Dockerfile scanned by caller-installed Checkov 3.3.9. Deployment manifests and platform-specific probes are outside this rule.
falsePositiveCauses: The deployment manifest defines an equivalent liveness or health probe.
The image is a one-shot job for which a continuous health check is not appropriate.

proposal.summary: Add a lightweight health check that reflects application readiness, with reviewed interval, timeout, start period and retries.

proposalRisks: A probe that starts too early, depends on an optional service or times out too quickly can restart a healthy application.
sideEffects: Startup time, dependency availability and temporary load spikes can cause false unhealthy states or restart loops.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun CKV_DOCKER_2 and verify the deployed platform observes the intended probe rather than only process liveness.
rules.functionalRetest: Start the service from cold state, test slow dependency startup and confirm healthy, degraded and failed states are reported as intended.
rules.rollback: Disable or relax the new probe if it restarts healthy instances, then restore monitoring while the readiness signal and timing are corrected.

alternatives: Set an approved non-root UID in the deployment runtime when the image must remain reusable, and enforce that override as code.
userDecisions: Confirm which directories must be writable and whether the service must bind a port below 1024.
rules.plainLanguage: The Dockerfile leaves the final container process running with the most powerful user inside the container.
rules.consequence: If the application is compromised, root privileges can make it easier to alter container files, bind privileged ports or abuse an unsafe runtime configuration.
rules.confidenceBoundary: Checkov rule CKV_DOCKER_8 matched the Dockerfile. A runtime USER override, rootless container engine or additional isolation may reduce the deployed impact; none was verified.
rules.applicability: Files named Dockerfile scanned by caller-installed Checkov 3.3.9. Other container build files and runtime manifests are outside stable coverage.
falsePositiveCauses: The deployment platform overrides the image user with an approved non-root UID.
The container needs a short root-only setup phase but the final runtime is constrained elsewhere.

proposal.summary: Create a dedicated runtime user, give it only the required files and directories, and set USER in the final image stage.

proposalRisks: The application may lose access to files, sockets or ports that currently depend on root ownership or privileges.
sideEffects: File permissions, bind-mounted volume ownership and low-numbered port binding can change; image build and startup may fail until ownership is explicit.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun the pinned Checkov rule and inspect the built image/runtime identity to confirm the application process uses the intended non-root UID.
rules.functionalRetest: Build and start the image, exercise startup, file writes, uploads, logs, health checks and every required network port.
rules.rollback: Revert the USER and ownership change if normal startup fails, keep the deployment restricted, and identify the exact permission before proposing a narrower change.

alternatives: Split publishing or deployment into a protected workflow with narrow permissions and keep build/test workflows read-only.
userDecisions: Confirm which jobs are allowed to publish releases, packages, attestations or deployments and which events may trigger them.
rules.plainLanguage: The workflow asks GitHub for write access to every available repository permission instead of only the operations its jobs need.
rules.consequence: If a workflow step or dependency is compromised, its token may be able to change repository content, releases, packages or other protected resources.
rules.confidenceBoundary: Checkov rule CKV2_GHA_1 matched top-level permissions: write-all. Event restrictions, job-level reductions, environment protection and actual token use were not evaluated.
rules.applicability: Root .github/workflows/*.yml and *.yaml files scanned by caller-installed Checkov 3.3.9. Reusable workflows outside that path are not claimed.
falsePositiveCauses: A tightly protected release workflow genuinely needs several write permissions, though write-all is still broader than necessary.
A reusable workflow receives an already restricted token from its caller.

proposal.summary: Set top-level permissions to read-only or none, then grant each job only the named write permissions it demonstrably uses.

proposalRisks: Release, package publication, deployment, pull-request comments or provenance jobs can fail when a required permission is omitted.
sideEffects: Existing release, publish and deploy jobs may return 403 errors until their exact contents, packages, deployments, id-token or pull-requests permissions are declared.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun CKV2_GHA_1 and inspect the effective token permissions for every triggered job and reusable workflow boundary.
rules.functionalRetest: Run representative pull-request, branch, release, package-publish and deployment workflows in a safe test path and verify all intended writes still succeed.
rules.rollback: Restore only the specific permission required by a failing job; do not return to write-all without recording an owner, reason and review date.

alternatives: Use same-origin requests or token-based non-cookie calls where cross-origin sessions are unnecessary.
userDecisions: List the browser origins that must use credentials in each environment.
rules.plainLanguage: One configuration says every website may make browser requests and also asks to include user credentials. That trust boundary is too broad or internally contradictory.
rules.consequence: A permissive effective policy can let an untrusted site read authenticated responses or can break legitimate browser requests in inconsistent ways.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule found origin: "*" and credentials: true in one object. It does not prove the object configures live CORS middleware or how a framework emits headers.
rules.applicability: Non-test, non-generated JavaScript and TypeScript containing a literal credentialed wildcard policy object.
falsePositiveCauses: The object is documentation or dead configuration outside excluded test paths.
Later middleware replaces the policy before sending a response.

proposal.summary: List the exact trusted origins and verify credentials are enabled only for endpoints that need browser sessions.

proposalRisks: An incomplete allowlist can block legitimate frontends, previews or local development.
sideEffects: Browser integrations from omitted origins will fail CORS checks.
rules.securityRetest: Request an owned authenticated endpoint from an untrusted test origin and verify the response is not readable.
rules.functionalRetest: Run login and API journeys from every approved production, preview and development origin.
rules.rollback: Restore the last known-good explicit allowlist if clients break; do not fall back to credentialed origin reflection or a wildcard.

alternatives: Record and verify an equivalent immutable dependency resolution artifact in CI.
userDecisions: Confirm which package manager and lockfile CI and production must use.
rules.plainLanguage: The project names its dependencies but does not record the exact versions used to build it.
rules.consequence: A later install can select different package versions, making security review and repeatable deployment less reliable.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule confirms that a supported manifest has no adjacent or applicable workspace lockfile. It does not prove a malicious dependency or exploitable vulnerability.
rules.applicability: Supported package.json or pyproject.toml project roots, including declared JavaScript workspaces.
falsePositiveCauses: A lockfile is generated only in a deployment system outside the audited source.
An unsupported package manager records resolution in another file.

proposal.summary: Generate and commit the lockfile used by CI and deployment.

proposalRisks: A newly generated lockfile can select versions that differ from the current deployment.
sideEffects: Dependency versions or transitive packages may change when the first lockfile is generated.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun the source audit and confirm the manifest is covered by a supported lockfile.
rules.functionalRetest: Run the normal install, build and project test commands using the committed lockfile.
rules.rollback: Revert the lockfile if the locked install or application tests regress, then reconcile the deployed dependency set before regenerating it.

alternatives: Use an approved narrow Gitleaks suppression for a proven non-secret fixture.
userDecisions: Confirm whether the match is a live credential and whether repository history may be rewritten.
rules.plainLanguage: A pinned Gitleaks rule matched secret-shaped material in Git history.
rules.consequence: If the value is a live credential, anyone with repository history access may be able to use it.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The match and redacted fingerprint are recorded. Credential validity, exposure and authorization are not tested.
rules.applicability: A Git worktree with the caller-installed tested Gitleaks version.
falsePositiveCauses: A test or revoked value matches a secret pattern.
A generated example intentionally resembles a credential.

proposal.summary: Validate privately, revoke any live credential and remove it from current and historical source where appropriate.

proposalRisks: History rewriting disrupts existing clones and references.
sideEffects: Credential rotation can interrupt services; history rewriting requires repository coordination.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun the pinned Gitleaks history scan and confirm the fingerprint is absent or covered by an approved suppression.
rules.functionalRetest: Verify every service using a rotated credential can authenticate and complete its normal health check.
rules.rollback: Do not reactivate a leaked credential; roll back application configuration to a separately issued valid credential if rotation breaks service.

alternatives: Use an approved narrow suppression for a proven non-secret fixture.
userDecisions: Confirm whether the match is live and which secret store should replace it.
rules.plainLanguage: A pinned Gitleaks rule matched secret-shaped material in the current files.
rules.consequence: If the value is live and later committed, built or shared, it may grant unauthorized access.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The match and redacted fingerprint are recorded. Credential validity and distribution are not tested.
rules.applicability: A readable project directory with the caller-installed tested Gitleaks version.
falsePositiveCauses: A placeholder or test value matches a secret pattern.
A local ignored file contains intentionally non-production data.

proposal.summary: Validate privately, revoke any live credential and remove it from source and build inputs.

proposalRisks: Credential rotation can interrupt dependent services.
sideEffects: Local development and CI need a replacement secret-injection path.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun the pinned Gitleaks directory scan and confirm the fingerprint is absent or approved.
rules.functionalRetest: Run dependent service authentication and the project tests with replacement credentials.
rules.rollback: Do not restore a leaked value; use a separately issued credential if the replacement fails.

alternatives: Use an asymmetric signing key from a managed KMS when the architecture supports it.
userDecisions: Confirm whether the literal is deployed, which consumers share it and whether planned mass reauthentication is acceptable.
rules.plainLanguage: A variable named like an authentication, session, JWT or cookie secret contains a fixed value in source code.
rules.consequence: Anyone who can read the source or artifact may forge tokens or sessions if the value is real and deployed.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule found a security-named assignment to a non-placeholder literal of at least 12 characters. It records only a length band; validity, history and deployment use are not tested.
rules.applicability: Non-test, non-generated JavaScript and TypeScript with narrowly recognized authentication-secret variable names.
falsePositiveCauses: The value is a deliberately fake fixture outside conventional test paths.
The constant is never used as an authentication secret.

proposal.summary: Validate privately, rotate any deployed value, inject the replacement from a secret store and remove it from source history where required.

proposalRisks: Rotating a signing or session secret can invalidate every active token or session.
sideEffects: Users may be signed out and services using the old secret may fail until coordinated.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun source and secret scans, verify the old key cannot authenticate, and confirm no report prints the value.
rules.functionalRetest: Run login, token issuance, refresh, cross-service verification and logout using the new secret source.
rules.rollback: Do not reactivate a disclosed secret; roll back application configuration only to a separately issued valid key if the new rollout fails.

alternatives: Isolate a required evaluator behind a strict allowlist and process boundary with no secrets or ambient privileges.
userDecisions: Confirm whether dynamic expressions are a product requirement and who controls their source.
rules.plainLanguage: The application turns runtime text into JavaScript instructions. If an attacker can affect that text, it can become code execution.
rules.consequence: A reachable attacker-controlled value may run commands in the browser or with the server process permissions.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule found a direct eval call or new Function constructor after masking comments and literals. It does not prove untrusted input reaches the argument or that the path runs.
rules.applicability: Non-test, non-generated JavaScript and TypeScript source files up to the configured file-size limit.
falsePositiveCauses: The argument is a constant controlled entirely by the application.
The code is unreachable in the deployed build.

proposal.summary: Replace dynamic evaluation with an explicit parser, lookup table or bounded expression library after tracing the argument source.

proposalRisks: Replacing an evaluator can change accepted expressions or plugin behavior.
sideEffects: Dynamic rules, templates or plugins may stop accepting previously valid input.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun the source audit and test that an untrusted expression is treated as data and cannot execute JavaScript.
rules.functionalRetest: Run the product journey that uses expressions, templates or plugins with representative valid inputs.
rules.rollback: Revert the parser integration if supported inputs regress, but keep the evaluator unreachable from untrusted input while selecting a compatible replacement.

alternatives: Use managed asymmetric signing keys when token consumers and rotation requirements support them.
userDecisions: Confirm whether the literal is deployed, which services share it and whether mass reauthentication is acceptable.
rules.technicalTerm: Inline session or JWT signing secret lead (CWE-798)
rules.plainLanguage: A recognized session or token library receives its signing secret as fixed text in source code.
rules.consequence: If the value is real and deployed, source or artifact readers may be able to forge sessions or tokens.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The bounded rule resolves a supported framework configuration and records only the literal length band. It does not retain the value or prove validity, deployment use or exposure.
rules.applicability: Direct Express Session, NextAuth/Auth.js configuration calls and NestJS JwtModule.register option objects in non-test JavaScript or TypeScript.
falsePositiveCauses: The value is a deliberately fake development constant outside conventional fixture paths.
A later runtime configuration replaces the literal before any signing operation.

proposal.summary: Validate privately, rotate any deployed value and inject the replacement from a protected secret source.

proposalRisks: Rotating the secret can invalidate active sessions or tokens across every application instance.
sideEffects: Users may be signed out and services sharing the old key may fail until rollout is coordinated.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun source and secret scans, verify the old key cannot authenticate and confirm reports contain no literal value.
rules.functionalRetest: Run login, session continuity, token issuance, refresh, verification and logout through every service using the key.
rules.rollback: Do not reactivate a disclosed value; switch to a separately issued fallback key if the new rollout fails.

alternatives: Use a separate non-sensitive browser-readable cookie while keeping authentication state in an HttpOnly Secure cookie.
userDecisions: Confirm which cookie carries authentication state, whether browser JavaScript must read it and where HTTPS terminates.
rules.plainLanguage: A recognized cookie or session API explicitly turns off browser protection that keeps the cookie on HTTPS or away from JavaScript.
rules.consequence: Depending on the disabled flag, a session cookie may travel over an unencrypted connection or become easier to steal through browser script injection.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule observes httpOnly:false or secure:false in a supported API option object. It does not infer missing flags, cookie purpose, effective proxy TLS or deployed middleware behavior.
rules.applicability: Direct supported JavaScript/TypeScript session and cookie API calls with explicit option literals.
falsePositiveCauses: The cookie is non-sensitive and intentionally readable by browser code.
A local-only HTTP development profile overrides the option in production.

proposal.summary: Identify the cookie purpose, enable HttpOnly for server-only cookies and Secure for HTTPS deployments using environment-aware framework configuration.

proposalRisks: Secure cookies do not work over plain HTTP and HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by frontend JavaScript.
sideEffects: Local development, embedded clients or frontend token-reading code may require an HTTPS setup or a different state flow.
rules.securityRetest: Inspect the owned response and verify the intended authentication cookie has the required Secure and HttpOnly attributes, then rerun the source audit.
rules.functionalRetest: Run login, refresh, logout, local development and any embedded-client journeys that depend on cookie behavior.
rules.rollback: Use an environment-specific local cookie policy if development breaks; do not disable production session-cookie protection globally.

alternatives: Record and manually review the excluded routes and controls while retaining the evidence gap as unknown.
userDecisions: Confirm whether the incomplete files or dynamic relationships are deployed and whether refactoring or a documented manual review is appropriate.
rules.plainLanguage: The project appears to use a supported web framework, but one or more files or relationships needed to map its routes and controls could not be analyzed.
rules.consequence: A route or authorization boundary may be missing from the route review until the incomplete source evidence is restored.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The route coverage ledger records bounded parser, module-linking or handler-resolution failures. It does not prove that an affected route is vulnerable or safe.
rules.applicability: JavaScript and TypeScript projects with detected Express, NestJS or Next.js App Router source or manifest evidence.
falsePositiveCauses: The incomplete file is unrelated to any deployed route despite living inside a supported framework project.
A dynamic framework construct is intentionally outside the documented static route contract.

proposal.summary: Review the named coverage reasons, restore parsable source or simplify the unresolved route relationship, then rerun before treating the route inventory as complete.

proposalRisks: Changing dynamic route registration or framework composition can alter routing order and runtime behavior.
sideEffects: Refactoring routes for static visibility can change path composition, middleware inheritance or framework startup behavior.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun the built-in audit until the route-security coverage entry is completed, then review the newly inventoried routes and controls.
rules.functionalRetest: Exercise framework startup and every affected route method/path after resolving parser or routing structure issues.
rules.rollback: Revert a route refactor if routing behavior regresses, keep the route evidence marked unknown, and document a manual review path.

alternatives: Use the identity provider's maintained verification middleware with pinned issuer and audience configuration.
userDecisions: Confirm the expected issuers, audiences, algorithms and session-expiry behavior.
rules.technicalTerm: Improper JWT signature or expiry verification lead (CWE-347)
rules.plainLanguage: Token verification explicitly allows an unsigned token or ignores expiry. A token that should be rejected may be accepted.
rules.consequence: If the option protects login or authorization, an attacker may impersonate a user or keep using an expired token.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule resolves direct jsonwebtoken imports/requires and finds verify calls with algorithms containing "none" or ignoreExpiration: true. It does not prove the call protects a live route.
rules.applicability: Non-test, non-generated Node.js JavaScript and TypeScript using direct jsonwebtoken bindings.
falsePositiveCauses: The call operates only on a non-security test token outside conventional test paths.
A later independent verification rejects the token before any security decision.

proposal.summary: Require the expected signed algorithm, issuer and audience, enforce expiry, and separate access-token and refresh-token validation.

proposalRisks: Previously accepted malformed, expired or differently issued tokens will stop working.
sideEffects: Existing sessions or integrations can require reauthentication or token configuration changes.
rules.securityRetest: Verify unsigned, wrong-algorithm and expired owned tokens are rejected while a valid token succeeds.
rules.functionalRetest: Run login, refresh, logout and authenticated API journeys for every supported identity provider.
rules.rollback: Restore service with a narrowly time-bounded compatibility path for correctly signed tokens only; never re-enable unsigned or expired-token acceptance.

alternatives: Replace the operating-system command with a library API or a narrowly allowlisted worker operation.
userDecisions: Confirm which shell features are required and which inputs can be influenced outside trusted code.
rules.plainLanguage: The server starts a command through a shell. A shell treats special characters as instructions, so unsafe input can change what runs.
rules.consequence: If request or job input reaches the command string, an attacker may read files, change data or run programs with the application permissions.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule resolves direct child_process imports/requires and finds exec/execSync or process calls with shell: true. It does not trace arguments or prove reachability.
rules.applicability: Non-test, non-generated Node.js JavaScript and TypeScript using direct child_process or node:child_process bindings.
falsePositiveCauses: Every command and argument is fixed by trusted code.
The path is an isolated build tool that never receives untrusted input.

proposal.summary: Trace command inputs, prefer execFile/spawn with shell disabled and pass each validated argument separately.

proposalRisks: Shell syntax, pipes, redirects and wildcard expansion stop working when the shell is removed.
sideEffects: Command quoting and platform behavior may change; existing automation can require explicit argument handling.
rules.securityRetest: Send shell metacharacters through the owned input path and verify they remain one inert argument, then rerun the source audit.
rules.functionalRetest: Run the normal export, conversion, media or job workflow that invokes the command on supported platforms.
rules.rollback: Revert the command adapter if valid jobs fail, but disable the untrusted route or restrict inputs until a shell-free form is working.

alternatives: Use an authenticated, access-controlled remote debugging tunnel for an explicitly approved incident window.
userDecisions: Confirm whether the script is used outside local development and whether remote debugging is required.
rules.plainLanguage: A package script asks the Node debugger to listen on every network interface.
rules.consequence: If that script runs on a reachable host, someone who reaches the debugger may inspect secrets or control the process.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The package command is present. The audit does not prove the script runs in production or that the debug port is reachable.
rules.applicability: String-valued package.json scripts using --inspect or --inspect-brk with 0.0.0.0 or [::].
falsePositiveCauses: The script is limited to an isolated local container.
Network policy makes the listener unreachable.

proposal.summary: Bind the inspector to loopback and keep debug scripts out of reachable production processes.

proposalRisks: Remote debugging workflows can stop working after the bind address changes.
sideEffects: Container or remote development debugging may require an explicit secure tunnel.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun the source audit and verify the deployed process exposes no public inspector listener.
rules.functionalRetest: Run normal start and approved debugging workflows in their intended environments.
rules.rollback: Restore the debug workflow only behind verified network isolation if approved debugging becomes impossible.

alternatives: Terminate TLS through an approved local trust proxy whose certificate is validated normally.
userDecisions: Confirm which private certificate authority or endpoint identity the client should trust.
rules.plainLanguage: The code tells Node.js not to verify who owns the HTTPS certificate. Encryption may remain, but the app can be talking to an impostor.
rules.consequence: A network attacker may intercept credentials or data on the affected outbound connection.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule found rejectUnauthorized: false or a literal NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED assignment to "0". It does not prove the setting runs in production.
rules.applicability: Non-test, non-generated Node.js JavaScript and TypeScript with explicit TLS verification-disable literals.
falsePositiveCauses: The setting is unreachable production-only dead code.
A local fixture uses an isolated certificate and the file was not placed under an excluded test path.

proposal.summary: Restore certificate verification and install the correct private CA or hostname configuration when a private service requires it.

proposalRisks: Private or local services with incomplete certificate chains will stop connecting.
sideEffects: Development, staging or private-service calls may fail until trust stores are configured.
rules.securityRetest: Connect through an owned invalid-certificate fixture and verify the client rejects it, then verify the valid certificate path succeeds.
rules.functionalRetest: Run all affected outbound integration health checks using the intended CA and hostname.
rules.rollback: Restore service availability with a valid temporary CA or endpoint configuration; do not globally disable verification.

alternatives: Map a small set of user-visible choices to fixed server-side commands without accepting command text.
userDecisions: Confirm which operations users may request and whether any shell feature is an actual product requirement.
rules.plainLanguage: Opengrep followed a value from a request query field through local variables into a function that starts a system command.
rules.consequence: If the request value reaches a shell without a strict allowlist, an attacker may run commands with the application permissions.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The pinned local taint rule observed a same-file source-to-sink path. It does not prove the route is reachable, the value is attacker-controlled in deployment or the command executes.
rules.applicability: JavaScript and TypeScript scanned by caller-installed Opengrep 1.27.0 with the bundled local ruleset.
falsePositiveCauses: The route is unreachable or request input is replaced by a strict fixed allowlist before execution.
The matched function is a compatible wrapper that never invokes a shell.

proposal.summary: Trace the owned route, replace shell execution with an API or execFile/spawn argument array, and validate each allowed operation.

proposalRisks: Shell features such as pipes, redirects, globbing and inline environment assignments will stop working.
sideEffects: Report, conversion or job workflows may need explicit argument and platform handling.
rules.securityRetest: Send harmless shell metacharacters through the owned request field and verify they cannot change the invoked program or arguments, then rerun Opengrep.
rules.functionalRetest: Run the normal report or job workflow with every supported option and platform.
rules.rollback: Revert the command adapter if valid jobs fail, but disable or restrict the untrusted route until a shell-free form works.

alternatives: Store an allowlisted ID-to-file mapping and never accept filesystem paths from requests.
userDecisions: Confirm the intended base directory, symlink policy, supported platforms and whether users need nested paths.
rules.plainLanguage: Opengrep followed a request value in one file into a filesystem read or write path.
rules.consequence: If path traversal is possible, an attacker may read private files or overwrite data outside the intended directory.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The pinned local taint rule observed a same-file JavaScript and TypeScript request-source-to-path sink path. It did not prove framework routing, validation bypass, runtime reachability, exploitability or a deployed endpoint.
rules.applicability: JavaScript and TypeScript scanned by caller-installed Opengrep 1.27.0 with the bundled local ruleset.
falsePositiveCauses: The route is unreachable or the request value is replaced by a strict fixed allowlist before the sink.
A wrapper or earlier canonicalization check may confine the final path to an owned base directory.

proposal.summary: Resolve the requested identifier under a fixed base directory, reject escapes after canonicalization and prefer server-generated identifiers over paths.

proposalRisks: Canonical path enforcement can reject symlinks, legacy relative paths or platform-specific path forms.
sideEffects: Download, upload, export or template features may need identifier and storage-layout migration.
rules.securityRetest: Use owned traversal and encoded-separator cases and verify no access outside the intended base directory, then rerun Opengrep.
rules.functionalRetest: Run valid download, upload, export and template journeys across supported platforms and storage layouts.
rules.rollback: Restore only a fixed reviewed mapping if valid files become unreachable; do not accept arbitrary relative or absolute paths.

alternatives: Remove caller-selected redirects and use a fixed post-action destination.
userDecisions: Confirm every legitimate external return origin and whether local paths alone satisfy the product flow.
rules.plainLanguage: Opengrep followed a request value in one file into a browser redirect target.
rules.consequence: An attacker may create a trusted-looking link that sends users to a phishing or malware site after it reaches the application.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The pinned local taint rule observed a same-file JavaScript and TypeScript request-source-to-redirect sink path. It did not prove framework routing, validation bypass, runtime reachability, exploitability or a deployed endpoint.
rules.applicability: JavaScript and TypeScript scanned by caller-installed Opengrep 1.27.0 with the bundled local ruleset.
falsePositiveCauses: The route is unreachable or the request value is replaced by a strict fixed allowlist before the sink.
The framework or an earlier validator may limit the target to a local path or approved origin.

proposal.summary: Accept only local relative paths or map approved destination names to fixed URLs; reject protocol-relative and unapproved absolute targets.

proposalRisks: External identity, payment or tenant-specific return journeys can stop working if their destinations are omitted.
sideEffects: Login, checkout and invitation flows may need an explicit return-target registry.
rules.securityRetest: Use owned absolute, protocol-relative and encoded redirect targets and verify rejection while approved local paths work, then rerun Opengrep.
rules.functionalRetest: Run login, logout, checkout, invitation and external identity return journeys for every approved destination.
rules.rollback: Add a reviewed exact destination if a valid journey fails; do not restore arbitrary redirect targets.

alternatives: Map user choices to fixed reviewed query templates without accepting SQL text.
userDecisions: Confirm the database driver, allowed dynamic identifiers and affected read/write journeys.
rules.plainLanguage: Opengrep followed a request value in one file into the query-text argument of a database execution call.
rules.consequence: If the value changes SQL structure instead of being passed as data, an attacker may read, alter or delete database records.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The pinned local taint rule observed a same-file JavaScript and TypeScript request-source-to-sql sink path. It did not prove framework routing, validation bypass, runtime reachability, exploitability or a deployed endpoint.
rules.applicability: JavaScript and TypeScript scanned by caller-installed Opengrep 1.27.0 with the bundled local ruleset.
falsePositiveCauses: The route is unreachable or the request value is replaced by a strict fixed allowlist before the sink.
The matched database wrapper may parameterize or reject the value before execution.

proposal.summary: Replace query-string construction with the driver or ORM parameter-binding API and allowlist any unavoidable identifier choices.

proposalRisks: Query behavior, placeholder syntax and result typing can change across database drivers.
sideEffects: Reports, filters or migrations may need explicit parameter and identifier handling.
rules.securityRetest: Use an owned input containing a quote and SQL metacharacters and verify it remains one bound value, then rerun Opengrep.
rules.functionalRetest: Run affected search, filter, reporting and write journeys with ordinary, empty and Unicode values.
rules.rollback: Revert the data-access wrapper if valid queries fail, but restrict the affected route until parameter binding works.

alternatives: Map a small user-visible destination name to fixed server-owned URLs.
userDecisions: Confirm required schemes, destination hosts, redirect behavior and whether private networks are ever legitimate.
rules.plainLanguage: Opengrep followed a request value in one file into an outbound HTTP request URL.
rules.consequence: If the server accepts arbitrary destinations, an attacker may reach internal services, cloud metadata or addresses that users cannot reach directly.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The pinned local taint rule observed a same-file JavaScript and TypeScript request-source-to-ssrf sink path. It did not prove framework routing, validation bypass, runtime reachability, exploitability or a deployed endpoint.
rules.applicability: JavaScript and TypeScript scanned by caller-installed Opengrep 1.27.0 with the bundled local ruleset.
falsePositiveCauses: The route is unreachable or the request value is replaced by a strict fixed allowlist before the sink.
A wrapper or earlier validator may restrict the final destination to an approved host and protocol.

proposal.summary: Parse the destination, allow only required schemes and exact hosts, resolve and recheck addresses, and block private or metadata ranges where they are not required.

proposalRisks: Strict destination policy can block redirects, proxies, IPv6 endpoints or customer-specific integrations.
sideEffects: Webhook, import and preview features may need an explicit destination allowlist and redirect policy.
rules.securityRetest: Use owned private-range, metadata and redirect-chain destinations and verify policy rejection, then rerun Opengrep.
rules.functionalRetest: Run every approved webhook, import, preview or callback destination including redirects and IPv6 where supported.
rules.rollback: Add reviewed exact destinations if integrations fail; do not restore arbitrary server-side URL fetching.

alternatives: Move the operation to an isolated worker that accepts a typed, allowlisted job rather than command text.
userDecisions: Confirm the allowed operations and whether shell parsing is required anywhere in the workflow.
rules.plainLanguage: Opengrep followed a Flask request value through local variables into subprocess execution with a shell enabled.
rules.consequence: If the request value is accepted without a strict allowlist, an attacker may run commands with the application permissions.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The pinned local taint rule observed a same-file Flask source-to-shell sink path. It does not prove the route is exposed, the code runs in production or exploitation succeeds.
rules.applicability: Python scanned by caller-installed Opengrep 1.27.0 with the bundled local ruleset.
falsePositiveCauses: The route is unreachable or the request value is replaced by a fixed allowlist before the sink.
A wrapper or monkey patch prevents the observed subprocess call from executing.

proposal.summary: Replace shell=True with an argument list or a library API and map request choices to fixed server-side operations.

proposalRisks: Shell expansion, pipes, redirects and quoting behavior will change.
sideEffects: Existing report or automation commands may require separate executable and argument handling.
rules.securityRetest: Send harmless shell metacharacters through the owned request field and verify they remain inert, then rerun Opengrep.
rules.functionalRetest: Run the normal Flask route or worker journey for every supported operation.
rules.rollback: Revert the subprocess adapter if valid jobs fail, but remove public access or restrict inputs until shell-free execution works.

alternatives: Store an allowlisted ID-to-file mapping and never accept filesystem paths from requests.
userDecisions: Confirm the intended base directory, symlink policy, supported platforms and whether users need nested paths.
rules.plainLanguage: Opengrep followed a request value in one file into a filesystem read or write path.
rules.consequence: If path traversal is possible, an attacker may read private files or overwrite data outside the intended directory.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The pinned local taint rule observed a same-file Python request-source-to-path sink path. It did not prove framework routing, validation bypass, runtime reachability, exploitability or a deployed endpoint.
rules.applicability: Python scanned by caller-installed Opengrep 1.27.0 with the bundled local ruleset.
falsePositiveCauses: The route is unreachable or the request value is replaced by a strict fixed allowlist before the sink.
A wrapper or earlier canonicalization check may confine the final path to an owned base directory.

proposal.summary: Resolve the requested identifier under a fixed base directory, reject escapes after canonicalization and prefer server-generated identifiers over paths.

proposalRisks: Canonical path enforcement can reject symlinks, legacy relative paths or platform-specific path forms.
sideEffects: Download, upload, export or template features may need identifier and storage-layout migration.
rules.securityRetest: Use owned traversal and encoded-separator cases and verify no access outside the intended base directory, then rerun Opengrep.
rules.functionalRetest: Run valid download, upload, export and template journeys across supported platforms and storage layouts.
rules.rollback: Restore only a fixed reviewed mapping if valid files become unreachable; do not accept arbitrary relative or absolute paths.

alternatives: Remove caller-selected redirects and use a fixed post-action destination.
userDecisions: Confirm every legitimate external return origin and whether local paths alone satisfy the product flow.
rules.plainLanguage: Opengrep followed a request value in one file into a browser redirect target.
rules.consequence: An attacker may create a trusted-looking link that sends users to a phishing or malware site after it reaches the application.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The pinned local taint rule observed a same-file Python request-source-to-redirect sink path. It did not prove framework routing, validation bypass, runtime reachability, exploitability or a deployed endpoint.
rules.applicability: Python scanned by caller-installed Opengrep 1.27.0 with the bundled local ruleset.
falsePositiveCauses: The route is unreachable or the request value is replaced by a strict fixed allowlist before the sink.
The framework or an earlier validator may limit the target to a local path or approved origin.

proposal.summary: Accept only local relative paths or map approved destination names to fixed URLs; reject protocol-relative and unapproved absolute targets.

proposalRisks: External identity, payment or tenant-specific return journeys can stop working if their destinations are omitted.
sideEffects: Login, checkout and invitation flows may need an explicit return-target registry.
rules.securityRetest: Use owned absolute, protocol-relative and encoded redirect targets and verify rejection while approved local paths work, then rerun Opengrep.
rules.functionalRetest: Run login, logout, checkout, invitation and external identity return journeys for every approved destination.
rules.rollback: Add a reviewed exact destination if a valid journey fails; do not restore arbitrary redirect targets.

alternatives: Map user choices to fixed reviewed query templates without accepting SQL text.
userDecisions: Confirm the database driver, allowed dynamic identifiers and affected read/write journeys.
rules.plainLanguage: Opengrep followed a request value in one file into the query-text argument of a database execution call.
rules.consequence: If the value changes SQL structure instead of being passed as data, an attacker may read, alter or delete database records.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The pinned local taint rule observed a same-file Python request-source-to-sql sink path. It did not prove framework routing, validation bypass, runtime reachability, exploitability or a deployed endpoint.
rules.applicability: Python scanned by caller-installed Opengrep 1.27.0 with the bundled local ruleset.
falsePositiveCauses: The route is unreachable or the request value is replaced by a strict fixed allowlist before the sink.
The matched database wrapper may parameterize or reject the value before execution.

proposal.summary: Replace query-string construction with the driver or ORM parameter-binding API and allowlist any unavoidable identifier choices.

proposalRisks: Query behavior, placeholder syntax and result typing can change across database drivers.
sideEffects: Reports, filters or migrations may need explicit parameter and identifier handling.
rules.securityRetest: Use an owned input containing a quote and SQL metacharacters and verify it remains one bound value, then rerun Opengrep.
rules.functionalRetest: Run affected search, filter, reporting and write journeys with ordinary, empty and Unicode values.
rules.rollback: Revert the data-access wrapper if valid queries fail, but restrict the affected route until parameter binding works.

alternatives: Map a small user-visible destination name to fixed server-owned URLs.
userDecisions: Confirm required schemes, destination hosts, redirect behavior and whether private networks are ever legitimate.
rules.plainLanguage: Opengrep followed a request value in one file into an outbound HTTP request URL.
rules.consequence: If the server accepts arbitrary destinations, an attacker may reach internal services, cloud metadata or addresses that users cannot reach directly.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The pinned local taint rule observed a same-file Python request-source-to-ssrf sink path. It did not prove framework routing, validation bypass, runtime reachability, exploitability or a deployed endpoint.
rules.applicability: Python scanned by caller-installed Opengrep 1.27.0 with the bundled local ruleset.
falsePositiveCauses: The route is unreachable or the request value is replaced by a strict fixed allowlist before the sink.
A wrapper or earlier validator may restrict the final destination to an approved host and protocol.

proposal.summary: Parse the destination, allow only required schemes and exact hosts, resolve and recheck addresses, and block private or metadata ranges where they are not required.

proposalRisks: Strict destination policy can block redirects, proxies, IPv6 endpoints or customer-specific integrations.
sideEffects: Webhook, import and preview features may need an explicit destination allowlist and redirect policy.
rules.securityRetest: Use owned private-range, metadata and redirect-chain destinations and verify policy rejection, then rerun Opengrep.
rules.functionalRetest: Run every approved webhook, import, preview or callback destination including redirects and IPv6 where supported.
rules.rollback: Add reviewed exact destinations if integrations fail; do not restore arbitrary server-side URL fetching.

alternatives: Apply an upstream-supported backport or isolate the affected feature until an upgrade is available.
userDecisions: Confirm whether the affected feature is used and whether update, isolation or time-bounded acceptance is appropriate.
rules.plainLanguage: OSV-Scanner linked a recorded dependency version to one or more public vulnerability advisories.
rules.consequence: If the application uses the affected code path, an attacker may be able to trigger the behavior described by the advisory.
rules.confidenceBoundary: Package identity, version and advisory IDs matched. Reachability, exploitability and local severity are not inferred.
rules.applicability: Supported lockfiles or dependency manifests accepted by the caller-installed tested OSV-Scanner version.
falsePositiveCauses: The vulnerable code path is not reachable in this product.
The advisory does not affect the product configuration or platform.

proposal.summary: Review advisory applicability, then update, replace or time-bound an explicitly owned suppression.

proposalRisks: Dependency upgrades can introduce API, behavior or transitive-dependency changes.
sideEffects: Build output, runtime behavior or compatibility can change after the dependency update.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun OSV-Scanner and confirm the advisory identity is absent or explicitly accepted with an owner and expiry.
rules.functionalRetest: Run the project test suite and the user journeys that depend on the upgraded package.
rules.rollback: Revert the dependency change if functional tests regress, then choose a supported mitigation without marking the advisory fixed.

alternatives: Generate hidden maps in a private build step and prevent them from entering public artifacts.
userDecisions: Confirm whether production error monitoring requires source maps and where private maps may be stored.
rules.plainLanguage: The build configuration asks for browser source maps that can reveal original source structure if they are published.
rules.consequence: Public maps can expose source code, comments and internal names that make later attacks easier.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The configuration enables map output. The audit does not prove a map was built or served publicly.
rules.applicability: Recognized Next.js, Vite, Nuxt, Svelte and Astro JavaScript/TypeScript configuration files.
falsePositiveCauses: Maps are uploaded only to an access-controlled monitoring service.
The production artifact pipeline removes maps before publication.

proposal.summary: Disable public production source maps or keep them only in an access-controlled monitoring service.

proposalRisks: Browser production debugging and readable error stack traces may become less useful.
sideEffects: Error monitoring needs a private source-map upload step to preserve symbolication.
rules.securityRetest: Rebuild and verify no public .map response or embedded source map is available, then rerun the source audit.
rules.functionalRetest: Run the production build, load the application and confirm error monitoring still symbolicates as intended.
rules.rollback: Restore private map generation if observability regresses, while keeping public artifact delivery blocked.

alternatives: Disable credentialed cross-origin access for public APIs that use no browser session or cookie.
userDecisions: Confirm the complete set of browser origins and whether credentials are required for each one.
rules.plainLanguage: The application appears to allow browser requests from every site while also allowing browser credentials.
rules.consequence: A browser client may expose authenticated responses to an unintended site if the effective middleware reflects or accepts that origin.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule observes paired wildcard-origin and credential literals in a supported framework configuration. Browser and middleware enforcement are not tested.
rules.applicability: Non-test Python with resolved Starlette/FastAPI or Flask-CORS calls, plus Django settings.py.
falsePositiveCauses: The framework rejects wildcard-plus-credentials at runtime.
The middleware is not attached to the deployed application.

proposal.summary: List the exact browser origins that need credentialed access and reject every other origin.

proposalRisks: Preview domains, mobile WebViews or customer-specific frontends can stop making browser requests.
sideEffects: Origin lists require environment-aware configuration and maintenance when frontend domains change.
rules.securityRetest: Verify an owned unlisted origin cannot read a credentialed response while every approved origin still can.
rules.functionalRetest: Run login and authenticated API journeys from each supported frontend, preview environment and custom domain.
rules.rollback: Add a missing exact origin after review; do not restore an unrestricted credentialed wildcard.

alternatives: For a token-authenticated API with no ambient browser credentials, separate it from cookie-authenticated routes and enforce its authentication and content-type contract.
userDecisions: Confirm whether each affected route uses browser cookies, which non-browser clients call it and what alternate control is intended.
rules.plainLanguage: A supported framework setting or exemption explicitly stops its normal check that a state-changing browser request came from the intended site.
rules.consequence: If the affected route uses browser cookies for authentication, another site may be able to make a signed-in user perform an unwanted action.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule observes an exact CSRF-disabled setting or recognized exemption. It does not prove route exposure, cookie authentication, missing alternate controls or exploitability.
rules.applicability: Django csrf_exempt decorators and resolved Flask-WTF or Flask-SeaSurf disabled settings/exemptions in non-test Python.
falsePositiveCauses: The exempt route uses no browser cookie authentication.
An independently verified origin/token check protects the exact state-changing operation.

proposal.summary: Map the affected route and restore framework CSRF protection or document and test an equivalent route-specific control.

proposalRisks: Existing forms, API clients, webhooks or cross-origin integrations may fail until they send the expected token or use the correct route.
sideEffects: Frontend forms and clients may need token retrieval, header or cookie changes.
rules.securityRetest: Send an owned state-changing request without the required CSRF proof and verify rejection while a valid request succeeds, then rerun the audit.
rules.functionalRetest: Run every affected form, authenticated API client, webhook and cross-origin integration with valid credentials and CSRF data.
rules.rollback: Temporarily restrict the route or authentication method if clients regress; do not restore an unbounded cookie-authenticated exemption.

alternatives: Use ast.literal_eval only for supported Python literal data, with input size limits.
userDecisions: Confirm which runtime expressions are legitimate product behavior and which inputs cross a trust boundary.
rules.plainLanguage: The program asks Python to treat a runtime value as executable code.
rules.consequence: If an attacker can influence that value, they may be able to run code with the application process permissions.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule observes a direct built-in eval or exec call. It does not prove input control, reachability or successful execution.
rules.applicability: Non-test, non-generated Python source with direct built-in eval or exec calls.
falsePositiveCauses: The call receives only a fixed trusted expression.
A local function shadows the built-in without an import the bounded rule can resolve.

proposal.summary: Replace runtime code evaluation with explicit parsing, a fixed operation map or a constrained data format.

proposalRisks: Previously accepted expressions or plug-in behavior can stop working.
sideEffects: The accepted input language becomes narrower and callers may need migration.
rules.securityRetest: Verify attacker-controlled owned input cannot select code or invoke functions, then rerun the source audit.
rules.functionalRetest: Run every supported expression, template or rule-processing journey with representative valid inputs.
rules.rollback: Restore only a reviewed fixed operation set if compatibility fails; do not restore evaluation of untrusted text.

alternatives: Use separate development and production settings with an explicit deployment-time environment selector.
userDecisions: Confirm the environment split, error-observability path and production deployment selector.
rules.plainLanguage: Flask or Django is explicitly configured to show developer debugging behavior.
rules.consequence: If this reaches production, error pages may expose source, settings or request data, and some debuggers can become a code-execution path.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule observes Flask debug=True/app.debug=True or Django DEBUG=True in settings.py. It does not prove the setting is active or publicly reachable.
rules.applicability: Non-test Flask source and Django settings.py files.
falsePositiveCauses: The file is used only in local development outside conventional test paths.
A later immutable production setting overrides the value.

proposal.summary: Make production debug mode fail closed and keep detailed errors in access-controlled logs.

proposalRisks: Developers may lose interactive error details and need local settings or log access.
sideEffects: Production error responses and local startup defaults can change.
rules.securityRetest: Trigger an owned error in a production-like environment and verify no debug page, source or secret is returned.
rules.functionalRetest: Verify local development debugging remains available only in the intended profile and production errors remain observable in logs.
rules.rollback: Restore local debug behavior in a development-only profile; never re-enable it in the production profile.

alternatives: Use managed key material or a platform secret service when supported.
userDecisions: Confirm whether the literal is deployed, which services share it and whether mass sign-out is acceptable.
rules.plainLanguage: A Flask or Django signing secret is written directly in source code.
rules.consequence: Anyone who obtains the source or artifact may be able to forge signed sessions or tokens if the value is real and deployed.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule observes a non-placeholder literal of at least 12 characters and records only its length band. Validity and deployment use are not tested.
rules.applicability: Non-test Flask app.secret_key assignments and Django SECRET_KEY assignments.
falsePositiveCauses: The value is an intentionally fake example outside conventional fixture paths.
The setting is replaced before any signing operation.

proposal.summary: Validate privately, rotate deployed values and inject the replacement from a secret store or protected environment setting.

proposalRisks: Rotation can invalidate every active signed session or token.
sideEffects: Users may be signed out and all application instances must switch keys in a coordinated rollout.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun source and secret scans, verify old signatures fail and confirm no report prints the value.
rules.functionalRetest: Run login, session continuity, logout and cross-instance session verification with the replacement key source.
rules.rollback: Do not reactivate a disclosed key; use a separately issued fallback key if rollout fails.

alternatives: Use local HTTPS so development exercises the same Secure-cookie behavior as production.
userDecisions: Confirm cookie purpose, browser-read requirements, HTTPS termination and environment-specific settings ownership.
rules.plainLanguage: A supported Django or Flask setting explicitly turns off HTTPS-only or JavaScript-blocking protection for a session-related cookie.
rules.consequence: The affected cookie may travel over an unencrypted connection or become easier to steal through browser script injection.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule observes an exact supported setting assigned False. It does not infer missing settings, production selection, proxy TLS behavior or cookie contents.
rules.applicability: Django settings.py and resolved Flask app.config assignments or update/from_mapping calls.
falsePositiveCauses: A development-only configuration is overridden by an immutable production setting.
The cookie is non-sensitive or HTTPS is unavailable only in an isolated local environment.

proposal.summary: Enable the required cookie flags in the production configuration and keep any local HTTP exception isolated to development.

proposalRisks: Secure cookies stop working over plain HTTP and HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by browser JavaScript.
sideEffects: Local development, frontend cookie access or proxy configuration may need changes.
rules.securityRetest: Inspect an owned production-like response and verify the authentication cookie carries the required attributes, then rerun the audit.
rules.functionalRetest: Run login, session continuity, logout, CSRF submission and local development flows through the configured proxy.
rules.rollback: Isolate a development-only exception if local workflows fail; do not globally disable production cookie protections.

alternatives: Replace the external command with a maintained library API.
userDecisions: Confirm whether shell syntax is required and which command choices or arguments users may control.
rules.plainLanguage: The program sends a command through a system shell, which gives special meaning to characters inside the command text.
rules.consequence: If untrusted text reaches the command, an attacker may add another command, read files or change data with the service permissions.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule resolves os/subprocess imports and observes a shell API or shell=True. It does not prove argument influence or runtime reachability.
rules.applicability: Non-test, non-generated Python using resolved os or subprocess process APIs.
falsePositiveCauses: Only fixed trusted command text reaches the shell.
The call is unreachable in the deployed application.

proposal.summary: Use an executable plus an argument array with shell disabled and validate any user-selectable values against a fixed allowlist.

proposalRisks: Shell features such as pipes, redirects, globbing and environment expansion will no longer work automatically.
sideEffects: Command quoting and platform behavior can change, so Windows and Unix paths may need separate handling.
rules.securityRetest: Pass owned arguments containing shell metacharacters and verify they remain one inert argument rather than executing another command.
rules.functionalRetest: Run the normal export, media, backup or administration journey that invokes the process on every supported platform.
rules.rollback: Roll back to a fixed, validated command wrapper if the array form breaks behavior; do not restore attacker-controlled shell text.

alternatives: Use a trusted local development certificate authority for development interception.
userDecisions: Confirm which internal CAs and interception proxies are legitimate in each environment.
rules.plainLanguage: The HTTP client is told to accept a server certificate without checking who issued it or which host it belongs to.
rules.consequence: Someone controlling the network path may impersonate the service and read or alter requests and responses.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule resolves Requests or HTTPX and observes verify=False on a supported call. It does not prove the path is deployed or interceptable.
rules.applicability: Non-test, non-generated Python with resolved Requests or HTTPX calls.
falsePositiveCauses: The call targets an isolated local fixture.
A development-only branch cannot reach production.

proposal.summary: Enable certificate verification and configure the required private CA bundle instead of disabling checks.

proposalRisks: Self-signed services, inspection proxies and incomplete certificate chains will fail closed.
sideEffects: Local development or enterprise proxy traffic may require CA installation and per-environment configuration.
rules.securityRetest: Verify a wrong-host or untrusted owned certificate is rejected and the intended trusted service still connects.
rules.functionalRetest: Run every outbound integration through production-like DNS, proxy and certificate-chain settings.
rules.rollback: Restore connectivity with a narrowly scoped trusted CA bundle; do not restore verify=False.

alternatives: Use JSON, MessagePack or another non-executable format with strict schema and size checks.
userDecisions: Confirm who creates the serialized data, whether old data must remain readable and how it will be migrated.
rules.plainLanguage: The program loads Pickle or Dill data, formats that can ask Python to construct objects and run code while loading.
rules.consequence: Opening attacker-controlled serialized data may run arbitrary code with the application process permissions.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule resolves pickle/dill imports and observes load or loads. It does not establish the source, integrity or reachability of the bytes.
rules.applicability: Non-test, non-generated Python with resolved Pickle or Dill load calls.
falsePositiveCauses: The bytes are generated locally and authenticated before loading.
The call is part of a trusted offline migration tool not shipped with the Web service.

proposal.summary: Use a data-only format and validate its schema; where legacy loading is unavoidable, authenticate bytes and isolate the loader.

proposalRisks: Stored sessions, caches, jobs or model artifacts may require migration.
sideEffects: Serialization fidelity and backward compatibility may change for Python-specific object types.
rules.securityRetest: Verify an owned malicious serialization fixture cannot trigger construction or code execution and rerun the source audit.
rules.functionalRetest: Read and write representative stored objects, queues, caches and imports using the replacement format.
rules.rollback: Keep legacy data read-only behind an isolated migration path; do not return untrusted Pickle or Dill loading to request handling.

alternatives: Use JSON with a schema when YAML features are not required.
userDecisions: Confirm whether custom Python YAML tags are intentional and which input sources are trusted.
rules.plainLanguage: The YAML loader explicitly allows Python objects instead of reading YAML as plain data only.
rules.consequence: A crafted YAML document may construct unexpected objects or run code if untrusted input reaches the loader.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule resolves PyYAML load and observes an explicit Loader or UnsafeLoader. It does not prove input trust or runtime reachability.
rules.applicability: Non-test, non-generated Python using resolved yaml.load calls.
falsePositiveCauses: The YAML input is immutable, trusted and authenticated.
A wrapper changes Loader semantics outside the bounded call.

proposal.summary: Use yaml.safe_load or SafeLoader and validate the resulting data shape and size.

proposalRisks: Python-specific YAML tags and custom object constructors will stop loading.
sideEffects: Existing configuration files using custom tags may need conversion.
rules.securityRetest: Verify Python-object YAML tags are rejected while ordinary configuration still parses, then rerun the audit.
rules.functionalRetest: Load every supported configuration and import sample, including aliases and multiline values.
rules.rollback: Add narrowly reviewed safe constructors for required tags; do not restore the unrestricted loader.

alternatives: Render a typed component model instead of accepting arbitrary HTML.
userDecisions: Confirm whether users need arbitrary HTML or only a bounded rich-text feature set.
rules.technicalTerm: Cross-site scripting sink lead in React (CWE-79)
rules.plainLanguage: React is told to render a value as real HTML instead of ordinary text. Unsafe HTML can run scripts in another user's browser.
rules.consequence: If an attacker controls unsanitized HTML, they may act as the signed-in user, read page data or alter what the user sees.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The rule found dangerouslySetInnerHTML with an __html property. It does not trace the value, recognize every sanitizer or prove browser reachability.
rules.applicability: Non-test, non-generated JSX and TSX, plus JavaScript/TypeScript files that contain the explicit React property.
falsePositiveCauses: The value is a fixed trusted literal.
A correctly configured sanitizer processes the value immediately before rendering.

proposal.summary: Prefer normal React text rendering; where HTML is required, sanitize at a documented trust boundary and restrict allowed elements and attributes.

proposalRisks: Sanitization or text rendering can remove formatting, embeds or custom attributes.
sideEffects: Rich-text appearance and supported content may change.
rules.securityRetest: Render a harmless script-marker payload through the owned input and confirm no script or event handler executes.
rules.functionalRetest: Open representative rich-text content and verify allowed formatting, links and accessibility behavior.
rules.rollback: Revert the renderer only if valid content breaks, while disabling untrusted HTML input until an allowlist is corrected.

alternatives: Keep a placeholder-only .env.example and inject real values through the deployment secret store.
userDecisions: Confirm whether the file contains live values and where each environment should obtain replacements.
rules.plainLanguage: A file named like a real environment configuration is present. The audit does not read its contents.
rules.consequence: If the file contains live credentials and is committed or published in a build artifact, an attacker may gain access to services or data.
rules.confidenceBoundary: Filename presence is a lead only. Repository tracking, contents, credential validity and public delivery are not established.
rules.applicability: Files named .env or .env.<environment>; documented example, sample, template, dist and defaults files are excluded.
falsePositiveCauses: The file contains only non-sensitive local settings.
The file is ignored and never copied into an artifact.

proposal.summary: Verify tracking and artifacts without printing values, then move live secrets outside source and builds.

proposalRisks: Changing environment injection can break local development, CI or deployment startup.
sideEffects: Developers and deployment jobs may need a new documented secret-injection path.
rules.securityRetest: Verify the file is absent from Git history and built artifacts, without exposing its contents, then rerun the audit.
rules.functionalRetest: Start the application in development and its deployment-like test environment with the replacement configuration path.
rules.rollback: Restore the prior configuration source only in a private environment if startup fails; do not recommit a live secret.

rules.plainLanguage: Some eligible files could not be read or the bounded scan stopped early, so missing findings cannot be treated as a clean result.
rules.consequence: A security issue may exist in files the audit did not inspect.
rules.confidenceBoundary: The coverage ledger proves an input was skipped, truncated or unreadable. It does not prove a vulnerability in that input.
rules.applicability: Every built-in source audit.
falsePositiveCauses: A deliberately excluded large or unreadable file is irrelevant to the application.
A conservative traversal limit stopped after all relevant files were already scanned.

proposal.summary: Review coverage reasons, restore readable inputs or raise an allowed bound, then rerun.

proposalRisks: Higher traversal limits consume more time and memory and may include unrelated files.
sideEffects: The next audit can take longer and produce additional findings.
rules.securityRetest: Rerun with the same subject and scope until all required source rules have completed coverage.
rules.functionalRetest: No product code change is required; confirm the audit still targets the intended project root.
rules.rollback: Restore prior traversal limits if resource use becomes unacceptable, and record the remaining evidence as unknown.

rules.plainLanguage: The built-in audit could not find a supported project manifest, so it could not establish which source checks apply.
rules.consequence: Relevant source risks may remain unchecked until the stack is identified.
rules.confidenceBoundary: This proves only that supported Node or Python manifests were not found inside the bounded traversal.
rules.applicability: Every built-in source audit.
falsePositiveCauses: The project uses an unsupported language or non-standard manifest.
Traversal limits excluded the manifest.

proposal.summary: Record the stack manually or add a reviewed adapter before drawing source conclusions.

proposalRisks: Expanding source scope can increase review time and expose additional local paths in sanitized evidence.
sideEffects: A new adapter or wider scope may add findings that were previously outside coverage.
rules.securityRetest: Provide a supported manifest or adapter and rerun until applicable source checks report coverage.
rules.functionalRetest: No product change is proposed; verify only that project discovery still identifies the intended root.
rules.rollback: Remove an incorrect stack override if it causes the wrong files or framework rules to be selected.

alternatives: Use the deployment platform secret store or protected environment injection and document only required variable names.
userDecisions: Confirm whether the file contains live values, which credentials require rotation and whether history rewriting is required.
rules.plainLanguage: Git records a file whose name is normally used for real environment configuration.
rules.consequence: If the file contains live credentials, anyone with repository or source-archive access may be able to reuse them against services or data.
rules.confidenceBoundary: Git confirms only that the sensitive filename is present in the current index. File contents are not read; credential presence, validity, history and artifact publication are not established.
rules.applicability: Git working trees containing tracked .env or .env.<environment> paths; example, sample, template, dist and defaults names are excluded.
falsePositiveCauses: The tracked file contains only public or placeholder configuration.
The current index contains a staged deletion that has not yet been committed.

proposal.summary: Inspect values privately, rotate any live credential, remove sensitive files from current and relevant historical source, and keep a placeholder example.

proposalRisks: Removing the file before replacing its configuration source can break development, CI or deployment startup.
sideEffects: Developers and deployment jobs may need a new secret-injection path; credential rotation can interrupt dependent services.
rules.securityRetest: Verify the path is absent from the current Git index and relevant history without printing values, then rerun the source audit.
rules.functionalRetest: Start, build and test every environment that previously loaded the file using the replacement secret source.
rules.rollback: Restore configuration through a private untracked file or secret store if startup fails; do not recommit a live credential.
